title: Rees-algebra bounds for the cohomology of the I^nF on a proper scheme
statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], $I\subseteq A$ an ideal, $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ a proper morphism [def-weil-proper-morphism], $\mathcal I=I\mathcal O_X\subseteq\mathcal O_X$ the image of $f^*\widetilde I\to f^*\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Spec}A}\to\mathcal O_X$ [def-nagata-extended-ideal], and $\mathcal F$ a coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module [pqf-def-coherent]. Put $\mathcal I^0\mathcal F=\mathcal F$ and, for $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal I^n\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal F$ be as in [def-weil-pbc-coherent-formal-module] (0), so that $\mathcal I^k\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal I^n\mathcal F$ for $k\ge n\ge0$. Fix $q\ge0$, write $M_n=H^q(X,\mathcal I^n\mathcal F)$ for $n\ge0$ (sheaf cohomology [pqf-def-cohomology]; an $A$-module, $a\in A$ acting through the image of $a$ in $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$), and for $k\ge n\ge0$ let $\mu_{k,n}:M_k\to M_n$ be the map induced by the inclusion $\mathcal I^k\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal I^n\mathcal F$. Then there is an integer $c\ge0$ such that (a) for all $n,m\ge0$ with $n+m\ge c$ one has $\mu_{n+m,n}(M_{n+m})\subseteq I^{m-e}M_n$, where $e=\max(0,c-n)$; and (b) for all $n\ge c$ one has $\operatorname{Ker}(\mu_{n,0})=\operatorname{Ker}(\mu_{n,n-c})$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application, line 5424), parts (2) and (3), with its proof (lines 5463-5538: the graded module M = (+)_n H^p(X, I^n F) is finite over the Rees algebra B = (+)_n I^n by Lemma 02O8, lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-times-F, line 5380; proof of (2) lines 5489-5497; the kernel K = (+)_n Ker(M_n -> M_0) is a graded B-submodule, finite since B is Noetherian, lines 5499-5509). Stacks writes I^nF for the image of f^*(I^n)~ (x) F -> F; this equals (I O_X)^n F as used here, since the image of f^*(I^n)~ in O_X is (I O_X)^n (on an affine open Spec B of X both are I^nB). Stacks' proof of (3) takes c = max of the degrees of generators of K ('max(d'_i, d'_j)', line 5506, a misprint for max_i d'_i); one c serves (a) and (b) together because both proofs work for every c at least the degrees of the generators (take the maximum of the two). Tags verified in tags/tags: 02OA, 02O8.

proof.text: (Setup: the products and their compatibilities.) Apply [lem-weil-pbc-cohomology-powers-ideal-rees-finite] to $A,I,f,\mathcal F,q$ (the same hypotheses, the same $\mathcal I^n\mathcal F$ and the same $M_n$): for $k,m\ge0$, $a\in I^k$ and $x\in M_m$ we have $a\star x=H^q(X,\lambda^{(m)}_a)(x)\in M_{m+k}$, where $\lambda^{(m)}_a:\mathcal I^m\mathcal F\to\mathcal I^{m+k}\mathcal F$ is multiplication by $f^\sharp(a)$; by its (1) $M=\bigoplus_nM_n$ is a $B$-module, $B=\bigoplus_kI^kt^k\subseteq A[t]$, with $\big(\sum_ka_kt^k\big)\cdot(x_m)_m=\big(\sum_{k+m=n}a_k\star x_m\big)_n$, and by its (2) $M$ is a finitely generated $B$-module. Since $H^q(X,-)$ is a functor on $\mathcal O_X$-modules [pqf-def-cohomology], equal composites of $\mathcal O_X$-linear maps give equal maps on $H^q$; this gives: (i) $\mu_{k,n}=\mu_{l,n}\circ\mu_{k,l}$ for $k\ge l\ge n\ge0$, the inclusions $\mathcal I^k\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal I^l\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal I^n\mathcal F$ [def-weil-pbc-coherent-formal-module] (0) composing to the inclusion. (ii) For $k\ge0$, $a\in I^k$, $m\ge m'\ge0$ and $x\in M_m$: $\mu_{m+k,m'+k}(a\star x)=a\star\mu_{m,m'}(x)$, because both $\mathcal I^m\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\lambda^{(m)}_a}\mathcal I^{m+k}\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal I^{m'+k}\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal I^m\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal I^{m'}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\lambda^{(m')}_a}\mathcal I^{m'+k}\mathcal F$ are the map $s\mapsto f^\sharp(a)s$. (iii) For $k,n\ge0$, $a\in I^k$ and $w\in M_n$: $\mu_{n+k,n}(a\star w)=aw$, the product of the $A$-module $M_n$: the composite $\mathcal I^n\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\lambda^{(n)}_a}\mathcal I^{n+k}\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal I^n\mathcal F$ is $s\mapsto f^\sharp(a)s$, which is $\lambda^{(n)}_a$ for $a$ viewed in $I^0=A$, and by (1) of [lem-weil-pbc-cohomology-powers-ideal-rees-finite] $H^q$ of the latter is multiplication by $a$ in the $A$-module $M_n$. (iv) For $x\in M_m$, $a,a''\in I^k$, $a'\in I^{k'}$: $(aa')\star x=a\star(a'\star x)$, $(a+a'')\star x=a\star x+a''\star x$, and $x\mapsto a\star x$ is additive (so $a\star0=0$): these are the $B$-module axioms of (1) applied to $at^k,a't^{k'},a''t^k\in B$, with $(at^k)(a't^{k'})=aa't^{k+k'}$, and to $x$ placed in degree $m$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, proof of Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application), lines 5465-5481 (M is a finite graded B-module by Lemma 02O8; the products B_n (x) M_m -> M_{n+m} are compatible with the transition maps)

proof.text: (Generation of $M$ in bounded degree.) By step 1, $M$ is generated as a $B$-module by finitely many elements $z_1,\dots,z_s$. Each $z_j$ is the finite sum of its homogeneous components $(z_j)_n\in M_n\subseteq M$, so the finitely many nonzero components, call them $x_1,\dots,x_t$ with $x_i\in M_{d_i}$, also generate $M$. Put $c_1=\max_id_i$ ($c_1=0$ if $t=0$). Claim: for every integer $c\ge c_1$, every $n\ge c$ and every $x\in M_n$, $x$ is a finite sum of elements $u\star z$ with $u\in I^{n-c}$ and $z\in M_c$. Indeed, viewing $x$ as an element of $M$ concentrated in degree $n$, $x=\sum_i\beta_i\cdot x_i$ with $\beta_i=\sum_kb_{i,k}t^k\in B$ ($b_{i,k}\in I^k$); comparing the components of degree $n$ by the product formula of step 1, $x=\sum_ib_{i,n-d_i}\star x_i$ with $b_{i,n-d_i}\in I^{n-d_i}$ (here $n\ge c\ge d_i$). Since $I^{n-d_i}=I^{n-c}I^{c-d_i}$, write $b_{i,n-d_i}=\sum_lu_lv_l$ with $u_l\in I^{n-c}$, $v_l\in I^{c-d_i}$; by step 1 (iv), $b_{i,n-d_i}\star x_i=\sum_lu_l\star(v_l\star x_i)$ with $v_l\star x_i\in M_{d_i+c-d_i}=M_c$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, proof of Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application), line 5483-5487, proof of (1): generators x_i in M_{d_i}; B_{n-c} M_c = M_n for n >= c >= max d_i

proof.text: (The kernels form a graded $B$-submodule.) For $n\ge0$ let $K_n=\operatorname{Ker}(\mu_{n,0})\subseteq M_n$ and $K=\bigoplus_nK_n\subseteq M$. For $k,m\ge0$, $a\in I^k$ and $y\in K_m$: by step 1 (i) and (ii) (with $m'=0$), $\mu_{m+k,0}(a\star y)=\mu_{k,0}(\mu_{m+k,k}(a\star y))=\mu_{k,0}(a\star\mu_{m,0}(y))=\mu_{k,0}(a\star0)=0$, so $a\star y\in K_{m+k}$. By the product formula of step 1, $\beta\cdot y\in K$ for $\beta\in B$, $y\in K$; $K$ is closed under addition. So $K$ is a $B$-submodule of $M$, and an element of $M$ lies in $K$ if and only if each of its homogeneous components does.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, proof of Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application), lines 5499-5501: K = (+) K_n is a graded B-submodule by the compatibility of products with transition maps

proof.text: (Generation of $K$ in bounded degree.) The ring $B$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-rees-algebra-noetherian] ($A$ Noetherian), and $M$ is a finitely generated $B$-module (step 1), so its $B$-submodule $K$ (step 3) is a finitely generated $B$-module by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-submodule-finite] applied to the Noetherian ring $B$. As in step 2, the finitely many nonzero homogeneous components of a finite set of generators of $K$ lie in $K$ (step 3) and generate $K$; call them $y_1,\dots,y_{t'}$, $y_i\in K_{d'_i}$, and put $c_2=\max_id'_i$ ($c_2=0$ if $t'=0$). Comparing degree-$n$ components as in step 2, every $x\in K_n$ ($n\ge0$) is $x=\sum_{i:\,d'_i\le n}b_i\star y_i$ with $b_i\in I^{n-d'_i}$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, proof of Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application), lines 5502-5505: as B is Noetherian and M is finitely generated, K is finitely generated; generators y_i in K_{d'_i}

proof.text: (The constant.) Put $c=\max(c_1,c_2)\ge0$, with $c_1$ from step 2 and $c_2$ from step 4. Then $c\ge c_1$, so the claim of step 2 holds for this $c$, and $c\ge d'_i$ for every generator $y_i$ of step 4.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, proof of Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application), lines 5489 and 5506: c as in the proof of (1), resp. c = max of the degrees d'_i; one c for both by taking the maximum

proof.text: (Part (a) when $n\ge c$.) Let $n\ge c$ and $m\ge0$; then $e=0$. Let $x\in M_{n+m}$. As $n+m\ge c$, step 2 writes $x$ as a sum of elements $u\star z$ with $u\in I^{n+m-c}$, $z\in M_c$. Since $I^{n+m-c}=I^mI^{n-c}$, write $u=\sum_ju'_ju''_j$ with $u'_j\in I^m$, $u''_j\in I^{n-c}$; by step 1 (iv), $u\star z=\sum_ju'_j\star w_j$ with $w_j=u''_j\star z\in M_n$. By step 1 (iii) (with $k=m$), $\mu_{n+m,n}(u'_j\star w_j)=u'_jw_j\in I^mM_n$. As $\mu_{n+m,n}$ is additive, $\mu_{n+m,n}(M_{n+m})\subseteq I^mM_n=I^{m-e}M_n$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, proof of Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application), lines 5494-5496, proof of (2), case c <= n: M_{n+m} = B_m B_{n-c} M_c = B_m M_n

proof.text: (Part (a) when $n<c$.) Let $0\le n<c$ and $m\ge0$ with $n+m\ge c$; then $e=c-n$ and $k:=m-e=n+m-c\ge0$. Let $x\in M_{n+m}=M_{c+k}$. By step 2 (degree $n+m\ge c$), $x$ is a sum of elements $u\star z$ with $u\in I^k$, $z\in M_c$. By step 1 (i), $\mu_{c+k,n}=\mu_{n+k,n}\circ\mu_{c+k,n+k}$ ($c+k\ge n+k\ge n$); by step 1 (ii) (with $m=c\ge m'=n$), $\mu_{c+k,n+k}(u\star z)=u\star\mu_{c,n}(z)$; by step 1 (iii), $\mu_{n+k,n}(u\star\mu_{c,n}(z))=u\,\mu_{c,n}(z)\in I^kM_n$. Hence $\mu_{n+m,n}(M_{n+m})\subseteq I^{m-e}M_n$. With step 6 this proves (a) for all $n,m\ge0$ with $n+m\ge c$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, proof of Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application), lines 5490-5493, proof of (2), case c > n: use M_c -> M_n and the compatibility of products with transition maps; image in I^{n+m-c}M_n

proof.text: (Part (b).) Let $n\ge c$. By step 1 (i), $\mu_{n,0}=\mu_{n-c,0}\circ\mu_{n,n-c}$, so $\operatorname{Ker}(\mu_{n,n-c})\subseteq\operatorname{Ker}(\mu_{n,0})=K_n$. Conversely let $x\in K_n$. By step 4, $x=\sum_ib_i\star y_i$ with $b_i\in I^{n-d'_i}$, $y_i\in K_{d'_i}$, $d'_i\le n$. By step 1 (ii) (with $k=n-d'_i$, $m=d'_i$, $m'=0$) and (iv), $\mu_{n,n-d'_i}(b_i\star y_i)=b_i\star\mu_{d'_i,0}(y_i)=b_i\star0=0$. Since $d'_i\le c$ (step 5), $n-d'_i\ge n-c$, and by step 1 (i) $\mu_{n,n-c}=\mu_{n-d'_i,n-c}\circ\mu_{n,n-d'_i}$ kills $b_i\star y_i$. Hence $\mu_{n,n-c}(x)=0$. So $\operatorname{Ker}(\mu_{n,0})=\operatorname{Ker}(\mu_{n,n-c})$ for all $n\ge c$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, proof of Lemma 02OA (lemma-cohomology-powers-ideal-application), lines 5506-5509, proof of (3): B_n y_i lies in Ker(M_{n+d'_i} -> M_n), hence K_n = Ker(M_n -> M_{n-c}) for n >= c

lean.statement: theorem cohomology_powers_ideal_application (A : Type v) [CommRing A] [IsNoetherianRing A] {X : Scheme.{v}} (I : Ideal A) (f : X ⟶ Spec (CommRingCat.of A)) [IsProper f] (F : X.Modules) (hF : RingedSpace.IsCoherent X.toRingedSpace F) (q : ℕ) : ∃ c : ℕ, (∀ (n m : ℕ), c ≤ n + m → LinearMap.range (idealPowerCohomologyMap f I F q (Nat.le_add_right n m)).hom ≤ I ^ (m - (c - n)) • (⊤ : Submodule A (idealPowerCohomology f I F q n))) ∧ (∀ n : ℕ, c ≤ n → LinearMap.ker (idealPowerCohomologyMap f I F q (Nat.zero_le n)).hom = LinearMap.ker (idealPowerCohomologyMap f I F q (Nat.sub_le n c)).hom)
